Question:
The letters \(P,\) \(Q,\) and \(R\) are entered into a \(20 \times 20\) table according to the pattern shown below. How many \(P\)s, \(Q\)s, and \(R\)s will appear in the completed table?

[Figure 1](figures/2023_AMC_8_Q16_question_fig1.svg)
Solution:
Along any row or column, the letters repeat in groups of three, with one \(P\), one \(Q\), and one \(R\). We can therefore count large regions in equal groups, leaving only a small corner to inspect.

Separate the lower-left \(2\times2\) corner from an \(18\times18\) square and two \(2\times18\) rectangles, as in the diagram. The picture shows the partition schematically, rather than at its actual scale.

[Figure 1](figures/2023_AMC_8_Q16_official_expansion_solution_fig1.png)

Each of the three larger regions can be divided into nonoverlapping strips of \(3\) cells along a row or column, because a side of length \(18\) is divisible by \(3\). Each strip contains one of every letter. These regions contain \(400-4=396\) cells altogether, so they contribute \(396/3=132\) of each letter.

In the lower-left \(2\times2\) corner, the letters are

\[
\begin{matrix}Q&R\\P&Q\end{matrix}.
\]

Adding that corner gives \(\boxed{133\ P\text{s},\ 134\ Q\text{s},\ 133\ R\text{s}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

For a repeating pattern, divide as much of the grid as possible into complete repeats, then count the leftover cells.
